title: AFC North Week 11 Recap: Aaron Rodgers released by the Steelers
summary: Drama is afoot in the AFC North following a week in which all three teams that played suffered losses. Cincinnati Bengals (7-3) The Bengals’ hot streak ended in Week 11 with a 22-20 loss to the Washington Commanders on Monday Night Football. Joe Burrow came back down to Earth following multiple games with at least […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - NOVEMBER 22: Aaron Rodgers #8 of the Pittsburgh Steelers and Head Coach Mike McCarthy of the Pittsburgh Steelers chat against the Philadelphia Eagles prior to an NFL football game at Lincoln Financial Field on November 22, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images Drama is afoot in the AFC North following a week in which all three teams that played suffered losses. Cincinnati Bengals (7-3) The Bengals’ hot streak ended in Week 11 with a 22-20 loss to the Washington Commanders on Monday Night Football. Joe Burrow came back down to Earth following multiple games with at least four touchdowns over the past six games, completing 28 of 40 pass attempts for 300 yards and two touchdowns against the Commanders. Both Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins were held in check as the superstar duo combined for 74 receiving yards and one touchdown on seven catches, while Mike Gesicki led the team with five catches for 77 yards. The ground game was quiet for the Bengals on Monday, as Samaje Perine led the way with just 26 rushing yards on six carries. Boye Mafe continues to look like a free agent steal for Cincinnati as he racked up three sacks against Washington, bringing his total to 9.5 for the season — a career best for the fifth-year edge rusher. Cleveland Browns (6-4) The Browns enjoyed a bye week following their win over the Houston Texans in Week 10. They will face the Las Vegas Raiders upon their return next Sunday as they fight to remain in playoff contention. Pittsburgh Steelers (6-4) The Steelers fell to 6-4 with a 19-16 loss to the Philadelphia Eagles in Week 11. Sunday’s game feels like an afterthought for Pittsburgh following the recent shocking news that the team first benched and then later cut quarterback Aaron Rodgers. Following his reported benching, the future Hall of Famer aired his frustrations regarding head coach Mike McCarthy during a Wednesday appearance on The Pat McAfee show. It was later announced that Rodgers had been released. Mason Rudolph will take over as the team’s starter now. This drama comes after DK Metcalf, the team’s highly-priced wide receiver, was ejected from Sunday’s game against the Eagles. Metcalf had just one catch for two yards before being thrown out. It was Max Hurleman who led the team with six catches for 61 yards and a touchdown. Rodgers led the team in rushing with just 29 yards on five carries. Alex Highsmith finished with two of Pittsburgh’s three sacks on backup quarterback Joe Milton. Baltimore Ravens (4-7) The Ravens’ sixth consecutive loss came in a 35-33 shootout with the Carolina Panthers. Jacoby Brissett once again gave Baltimore a fighting chance, completing 24 of 37 pass attempts for 276 yards, one touchdown, and an interception on the final drive of the game. The rushing attack showed life after picking up just 16 yards on the ground a week ago against the Los Angeles Chargers. Derrick Henry had his best game in over a month with 94 rushing yards and a touchdown on 13 carries, though he did lose a fumble on a catch at the start of the fourth quarter. Justice Hill’s strong day was also marred by a costly fumble that went through the back of the end zone for a touchback. It did not stop there, though, as LaJohntay Wester put the ball on the ground two more times on punt returns, losing one that led to immediate points for the Panthers. Wester has since been released. Zay Flowers led the team in catches and receiving yards with eight for 97, while Rashod Bateman caught a 52-yard touchdown on a trick play. Mike Green was a standout for Baltimore’s defense once again this week, notching two sacks for the second game in a row. T.J. Tampa was another bright spot during an otherwise disappointing defensive effort, as the third-year cornerback intercepted Bryce Young in the end zone to end Carolina’s drive.

title: Pittsburgh Steelers vs. Denver Broncos, Black Friday NFL fan discussion
summary: Well, here we go, Rumblers! Fans of the Buffalo Bills are still waiting to come back down from their emotional high following a crazy win at home against the Kansas City Chiefs. It’s been a Thanksgiving to remember with a trio of turkey day games that weren’t decided until the final play. Now there’s today’s […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PA - NOVEMBER 22: Pittsburgh Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers #8 reacts during the game between the Philadelphia Eagles and the Pittsburg Steelers on November 22nd, 2026 at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia, PA. (Photo by Terence Lewis/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Well, here we go, Rumblers! Fans of the Buffalo Bills are still waiting to come back down from their emotional high following a crazy win at home against the Kansas City Chiefs. It’s been a Thanksgiving to remember with a trio of turkey day games that weren’t decided until the final play. Now there’s today’s game, which might be more interesting due to the drama unfolding in Pennsylvania. The 6-4 Pittsburgh Steelers are set to host the 8-2 Denver Broncos in a matchup with pretty big playoff stakes. However, all anyone can talk about is Aaron Rodgers snitching on head coach Mike McCarthy. However you may feel about the entire situation, it’s indisputable that Rodgers appears to have violated an unspoken NFL code. Now, Rodgers is left to wallow in the darkness while waiting for the ayahuasca to take effect and numb away the pain — self-inflicted pain, mind you. Has Rodgers permanently tarnished his certain and future Pro Football Hall of Fame inclusion? They say time heals all wounds, but Rodgers is prone to endlessly tearing away beneficial scabs. For many in Bills Mafia, this soap opera is a bit personal now. Instead of showing fans the Goo Goo Dolls’ halftime performance at Highmark Stadium, NBC decided to conduct an interview between Mike Tirico and Mike Tomlin focused on Rodgers and the Steelers. This, despite every other game from Wednesday night until late-day Thursday showing their game’s halftime performance. It was an unusual public relations misstep by the network, and one that came during one of the nation’s biggest holiday viewing windows. Yet you know that’s why NBC ran with the Rodgers-Steelers drama over a feel-good moment for Buffalo and Western New York. Savvy internet users will have found the Goo Goo Dolls’ halftime show by now, but here’s a high-def video shared by One Bills Drive for those of you who wanted to see it: Back to today’s game. Guess who Bills fans should root on to victory: Pittsburgh. Yes, it’s true. A Broncos loss would drop them to 8-3, thus creating a bit of separation between Buffalo’s 10-1 first place AFC record and another potential playoff foe. During his halftime interview, Tomlin called the Steelers a dumpster fire more than once. It’s true, and most should have seen it coming with Rodgers in the picture. Now, Pittsburgh will try to rally a once-promising season back on track toward a playoff birth. Instead of the over-the-hill Rodgers, quarterback Mason Rudolph has been tasked with righting the ship. This one could go one of two ways: The recent drama could serve to completely unravel the team, and usher in a move to can McCarthy before season’s end. Or, McCarthy and the team could prove Rodgers and the court of public opinion wrong by using this nightmare as a chance to do big things. I wouldn’t expect Broncos head coach Sean Payton to oblige the ask. Denver is in a fight to win the AFC West, and victory today sends them to first place over the Chiefs. How do you see this one playing out? With that, here’s your open thread for Steelers vs. Broncos on Black Friday. As always, be kind to one another — and in all things… Go Bills!

title: Overturning Rashee Rice fourth-quarter catch to incomplete was correct call
summary: Of course a Buffalo Bills site would run this article with this headline, right? Really though, I wanted to get the bottom of the controversial call that went in the Bills’ favor on the Chiefs second-to-last possession in the fourth quarter of Buffalo’s epic 13-10 walk-off win over Kansas City on Thanksgiving night. And I’ve […]
full_text: Of course a Buffalo Bills site would run this article with this headline, right? Really though, I wanted to get the bottom of the controversial call that went in the Bills’ favor on the Chiefs second-to-last possession in the fourth quarter of Buffalo’s epic 13-10 walk-off win over Kansas City on Thanksgiving night. And I’ve reached a very definitive conclusion. The review was correct. Rashee Rice did not catch the football. We have to dismiss the “eye test” here, because NFL’s rulebook is the governing guide to the game. That distinction first has to be established. As convoluted as it may be to some, this is the official rule. It’s a catch if a player: My good bud Joe Goodberry — a wildly popular and insightful Bengals analyst and Niagara Falls native + resident — explained Friday on Twitter. Here’s the start of his thread, which featured a civil disagreement (yes, they’re possible!) between Joe and Sam Monson of the 33rd Team: Per the written rules, the Parker Washington catch wasn't a catch either. I'm an idiot for having the rulebook downloaded on my phone, I know. And I'm even stupider for trying to explain it. I think it's actually written pretty clearly. Just like I didn't think Ja'Marr… — Goodberry (@JoeGoodberry) November 27, 2026 Instead of pasting each component of the lengthy back-and-forth between Goodberry and Monson, I’ll summarize the correct interpretation of the rule here. Rice satisfied (a) and (b) on this play. He secured control of the ball first before hitting the ground, then his elbow hit the ground while in control. But, scroll up to check (c) again. Rice did not “perform an act common to the game” — because he was simply falling to the turf, not a common act — therefore he must survive the ground. So, (a), (b), and (c) together were not fulfilled. Had they been, it would have been a catch. Case close. Precisely what occurred on the Rice play is clearly defined in section (2) of the rule. It specifies if (a) and (b) are satisfied, a player does not “survive the ground” if he hits the ground and loses control of the ball, there is no possession if the ball hits the ground before he regains control. That is exactly what happened on the play. Was it an egregious loss of control from Rice? Just an fyi on why this is a good call for no completion: Rice doesn't maintain control. The hand slips UP the ball and stops going up the ball when the ball contacts the ground. Meaning the ground is what stops the ball movement and what allows him to gain possession If he had… — Rob (@oscolaidhe55) November 27, 2026 No. But any degree of losing control counts if the ball hits the ground in the process. Which is why the NFL got this call right.

full_text: The Buffalo Bills beat the Chiefs 13-10 in dramatic fashion in Week 12 at Highmark Stadium to provide all of Western New York and Bills fans everywhere an idyllic ending to Thanksgiving. The Bills are now 10-1, which is tied for the best start in franchise history. These are my takeaways from Buffalo’s victory. Buffalo’s special teams were incredible From Tyler Bass to Greg Dortch to Buffalo’s coverage units, it was a special-teams masterclass from the Bills in a contest that felt likely to come down to special teams. I cannot and will not forget Joe Andreessen either. He’s become a special-teams ace. Dortch averaged almost 12 yards per punt return. On his final return of the night, his extra cut at the 44-yard line was HUGE, of course. Tommy Domann Jr. settled in after acclimating to the abysmal weather with some gorgeously placed punts, and of course, Tyler Bass was otherworldly. This sums up Bass’ memorable evening: Tyler Bass is the first kicker in NFL history with a game-tying 54+ yard FG and a game-winning 54+ yard FG in the 4th quarter of the same game. pic.twitter.com/AVRnDqoluO — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) November 27, 2026 The addition of special teams coordinator Jeff Rodgers has been a low-key godsend, and the players on Buffalo’s special teams unit are magnificent. And they were magnificently important to this win. Buffalo’s clock management also rocked The moment Patrick Mahomes dropped that shotgun snap, the absolute correct move for the Bills was to call timeout. And once they committed to it, they had to stick with it. And they did. Run play. Instant timeout. Then the minuscule miscommunication between Patrick Mahomes and Travis Kelce on the third-down incompletion. At the start of his head-coaching tenure, there were some questionable-at-best clock management decisions from Brady. And he’s learned from them. That’s vital. In today’s NFL, the foot needs to remain on the gas pedal, at all times. Particularly in a contest like that one. Hats off to Brady and his clock-management team for their work at the end of that game. The quality of the defensive effort cannot be overstated The weather is the latest asterisk, right? Kind of. But the Chiefs went punt, punt, punt, punt, field goal, touchdown, punt, missed field goal, punt, punt in this game. That’s seven punts. In the Mahomes era, which begins when he assumed the starting quarterback gig in 2018, Kansas City had just two other games with seven or more punts before this loss to the Bills. And it was a group effort, which is vital. For as much as Greg Rousseau has become a burgeoning superstar on the defense, everyone contributed. Michael Hoecht had two pressures on seven pass-rush snaps. Davison Igbinosun played awesomely. So did Maxwell Hairston in place of Christian Benford. The linebackers were stellar. Cole Bishop and Amani Hooker complemented each other perfectly. And everybody tackled outstandingly — only four misses all game. Oh, and Jim Leonhard called a fantastic contest from the booth. Well-timed blitzes. Good mix of man and zone. I cannot stress how impressed I was with Buffalo’s collective defensive effort in this game. Josh Allen needs to be better And if there’s one player or one area of the team that needs to improve for the 10-1 Bills, you want it to be Allen. His eight-plus season sample size with countless ridiculous plays and incredible performances galore indicate he will return to normal form when it matters most. The weather can’t be ignored from this game, and he had two interceptions off tips but did miss — and wasn’t particularly close — on a few routine-ish throws. He did lean on his legs again, which is a great sign, and that 17-yard scamper after spinning out of a sack was vintage Allen. Down the stretch and in the postseason, the Bills will likely need their superstar quarterback to be noticeably better, and I’m banking on Allen being Allen in those scenarios. Hat tip to the Bills offensive line James Cook was a workhorse in this contest with 117 yards on 32 carries. He accumulated hard yardage too. Three-to-five yards at a time. His long run was only 10 yards. And that old-school stat line was made possible by the diligent work by Buffalo’s five-man offensive front. Connor McGovern — whom I believe is playing at an All-Pro level — was ridiculous against the Chiefs interior defensive line. Alec Anderson got after it at left guard — which is seemingly always the case — and O’Cyrus Torrence routinely moved people in the run game. Another constant. Of course, Dion Dawkins and Spencer Brown were agile bulldozers paving lanes for Cook on a regular basis too. Remember, going into this game, the Chiefs defense had the sixth-best EPA per run allowed in the NFL. And the Bills were able to stay committed to the rushing attack all evening in a game that called for it.
author: Chris Trapasso

title: Buffalo Bills match best start in franchise history at 10-1
summary: We’re 11 games into the 2026 NFL season, and the Buffalo Bills have lost just once. With their 13-10 win over the Kansas City Chiefs on Thanksgiving night, the Bills have matched the best 11-game start in franchise history.  It was ugly. It was wet. It was cold. It was supposed to be an epic showdown […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - NOVEMBER 26: Tommy Doman Jr. #39 and Tyler Bass #16 of the Buffalo Bills warm up before the game against the Kansas City Chiefs at Highmark Stadium on November 26, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Joe Hrycych/Getty Images) | Getty Images We’re 11 games into the 2026 NFL season, and the Buffalo Bills have lost just once. With their 13-10 win over the Kansas City Chiefs on Thanksgiving night, the Bills have matched the best 11-game start in franchise history. It was ugly. It was wet. It was cold. It was supposed to be an epic showdown between two NFL MVP quarterbacks. But in the end, it was a 57-yard field goal in the rain that sailed straight and true off the foot of Tyler Bass as the clock expired. BILLS WIN!!!!!!!!!!!!! @MandT_Bank | #KCvsBUF pic.twitter.com/y23fz9iBod — Buffalo Bills (@BuffaloBills) November 27, 2026 In 67 seasons of Bills football, only three other teams have made it through their first 11 games with just one loss. If you’re looking for a little reason to be optimistic about where this season could be headed, let’s take a look at what those three teams went on to accomplish. The 1964 Bills, under head coach Lou Saban, finished their regular season with a 12-2 record before defeating the San Diego Chargers, 20-7, to win the first of back-to-back AFL championships. It would be another 24 years before Buffalo got off to another 10-1 start. In 1988, Marv Levy’s Bills finished the regular season at 12-4, winning the AFC East for the first time since 1980 and making it to the AFC Championship Game, where they lost to the Cincinnati Bengals. Three years later, the Bills were at it again. The 1991 team turned its 10-1 start into a 13-3 regular-season record and made the second of Buffalo’s four consecutive Super Bowl appearances. Now we can add Joe Brady’s 2026 team to that list. Brady has won 10 of his first 11 games as an NFL head coach. To put that into perspective, two of the more successful first-year head coaches in recent NFL history, Jim Harbaugh (2011, San Francisco 49ers) and Kevin O’Connell (2022, Minnesota Vikings), were both 9-2 through their first 11 games. Of course, getting to 10 wins hasn’t always looked the same for this year’s Bills. Early in the season, we were talking about how much the offense was going to have to do to compensate for the defense. Over the past few weeks, it’s been the defense that’s given us some of the biggest reasons to believe this team could be playing football into February. With six games remaining on Buffalo’s regular-season schedule, the franchise record of 13 regular-season wins is well within reach. And while the Bills have won 13 games on several occasions, they’ve never won 14. There’s still plenty of work to be done, beginning with a trip to Foxborough next week. But on Thanksgiving night, Bills Mafia can enjoy something it hasn’t experienced in 35 years — a 10-1 football team.
author: Rachel Auberger

title: Buffalo Bills QB Josh Allen ties Russell Wilson’s wins record
summary: For all the records Buffalo Bills quarterback Josh Allen has broken lately, this might be one that means a little more to him. After all, if you’ve listened to enough of Allen’s postgame press conferences, you know there’s one statistic he cares about more than any other — wins.  With Buffalo’s 13-10 win over the […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - NOVEMBER 26: Josh Allen #17 of the Buffalo Bills scrambles in the first quarter against the Kansas City Chiefs at Highmark Stadium on November 26, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Timothy T Ludwig/Getty Images) | Getty Images For all the records Buffalo Bills quarterback Josh Allen has broken lately, this might be one that means a little more to him. After all, if you’ve listened to enough of Allen’s postgame press conferences, you know there’s one statistic he cares about more than any other — wins. With Buffalo’s 13-10 win over the Kansas City Chiefs on Thanksgiving night, Allen has now won 98 regular-season games, tying Russell Wilson for the most wins by a starting quarterback in his first nine NFL seasons. Wilson, who entered the league in 2012, never had a losing season during his first nine years with the Seattle Seahawks. He won double-digit games in eight of those nine seasons, including a career-high 13 in 2013. Allen, on the other hand, won just five games as a rookie in 2018. A year later, the Bills were back in the playoffs, and they haven’t had a losing season since. In fact, Buffalo extended its franchise record to eight consecutive winning seasons just last week with a win over the Miami Dolphins. Allen moved past Patrick Mahomes (95) on this particular list two weeks ago when the Bills beat the New York Jets. Now, having picked up another win at Mahomes’ expense, Allen has caught Wilson, too. Allen completed just 10-of-21 passes for 81 yards while adding 43 yards on the ground. The real hero of the night was Tyler Bass who scored seven of the team’s 13 points – including the game winning field goal from 57 yards. But football is a team sport, and Allen’s contribution still counts. And the win is his to claim. The Bills will be in New England next week, where Allen will have his first opportunity to take sole possession of the NFL record. Allen still has six regular-season games left in his ninth season. That gives him some time to make life a little more difficult for the next quarterback chasing this record.
author: Rachel Auberger

title: Bills vs. Chiefs Week 12 postgame analysis: Buffalo’s defense too much for KC
summary: The Buffalo Bills beat the Kansas City Chiefs 13-10 on Thanksgiving night at Highmark Stadium, with Tyler Bass’s 57-yard field goal sailing through straight as an arrow as time expired. Want to know what I was thinking as this one unfolded? Read on below for that and more! 1st Half 2nd Half Final Thoughts I’ve […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - NOVEMBER 26: Josh Allen #17 of the Buffalo Bills runs with the ball in the third quarter against the Kansas City Chiefs at Highmark Stadium on November 26, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Joe Hrycych/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills beat the Kansas City Chiefs 13-10 on Thanksgiving night at Highmark Stadium, with Tyler Bass’s 57-yard field goal sailing through straight as an arrow as time expired. Want to know what I was thinking as this one unfolded? Read on below for that and more! 1st Half Bills starting with the ball again. 11th straight game doing so, but first drives haven’t been good recently. PA on 1st down. With this weather, no reason not to expect the normal under-center, heavy offense to begin with. (35 degrees, rain, and 20 mph winds) Eh, not a great 1st drive, again. Run game is slowed down, and Josh Allen can’t connect with Khalil Shakir on 3rd down. Punt isn’t good, touchback. (Opening drive: 8 plays, 29 yards, punt) Great first drive by the defense. Forces 3rd and 1, and Bradley Chubb appears with a great stop in the backfield. Chubb has to be better than he’s been so far, especially with the attention his DL teammates are getting. (Chubb: 2 tackles, 1 tackle for loss; Chiefs’ first drive: 3 plays, 7 yards) 3 and out. Poor execution on a QB run on 2nd down. I liked the idea, though. Josh tries DJ Moore deep on 3rd down but nowhere near a completion here. This time the punt is good, and Patrick Mahomes will have his back against the wall. (Moore: 2 catches on 6 targets, 15 yards) Bills’ D forcing another 3rd and 1 and being able to win there. Chiefs go PA this time, and Buffalo was ready for it, making Mahomes hesitate. Great job by Jim Leonhard and his unit on 3rd down so far. (Chiefs finished 2-of-11 on 3rd down) Awful punt by the Chiefs. In a rough game so far, Buffalo’s winning the field position battle. The offense will start from midfield. James “Jimbo” Cook starts to get his yards. Vital today. (Cook: 32 carries, 117 yards, 1 TD) 3rd down, George Karlaftis flies by Spencer Brown, but Josh is ready. Awesome move, up in the pocket, breaking the sack and finding Shakir. Small window throw. Bills inside the 13-yard line. (Karlaftis: 3 tackles, no sacks) Ty Johnson can’t get the 1st down after receiving the pass on 3rd down. 4th and 1, and the Bills go for it with Cook running to the right — the new trend to balance the always-to-the-left Josh Allen tush pushes. Jimbo gets the job done. 1st and goal Buffalo. (Bills: 1-for-1 on 4th down; Ty Johnson: 2 catches, 12 yards) The refs start to do their thing for KC. 2nd and inches, a clear neutral zone infraction by the Chiefs’ defense somehow becomes a false start on Buffalo. It doesn’t matter. Cook runs for the TD next and tosses the ball to the ref as he makes it to the end zone. Looked like a “try something now” toss, and I like it. At the same time, not evident enough to draw a flag. Well done, Jimbo. 10th consecutive game with a TD by Cook. (Cook: 5-yard TD run, his 11th TD of the season) Jordan Hancock getting a shot as the “Travis Kelce stopper,” without Christian Benford around. Got manhandled by the vet. I’d like to see Davison Igbinosun getting a shot there. (Kelce: 4 catches for 71 yards, all of it before halftime) Another great defensive drive by Buffalo. Mahomes misses Josh Downs wide open on 3rd down. Awful punt next, Matt Araiza with a fumble before he could finally kick it out of bounds. The Chiefs are struggling to deal with the weather. (Downs: 1 catch on 4 targets, 13 yards) The Bills’ O-line is on a good drive. The OL has played great, imposing themselves and giving Cook some room to work with. Buffalo’s already in the red zone. (Bills: 43 carries, 166 yards) Josh Allen with his first major mistake today. Play-action rollout to his left, but nobody’s open. He tries Dawson Knox, who slips as he tries to come back for the ball. Replay shows Karlaftis could tip the pass, allowing Alohi Gilman to be able to dive for the INT. Huge missed opportunity. (Knox: 0 catches on 1 target) Buffalo’s D continues to impress. Forces 3rd and 12 and stops the Chiefs’ screen on 3rd down. The offense has to capitalize on the strong start by the D. Poor offensive drive by Buffalo, and the Chiefs will have a 2 min drive opportunity. This time Tommy Doman is the one to shank the punt. KC will start from the 40. Kelce moves the chains a couple of times, and Rashee Rice appears with another 1st down. Mahomes converts a 4th and 1 with his legs, but Terrel Bernard makes him pay for the decision with a hit. (Bernard: 6 tackles) Cole Bishop now with a big hit after Kelce catches the pass to put the Chiefs on the 9-yard line with 9 seconds left. 1st and goal Chiefs. (Bishop: 5 tackles, all solo) IGB holds his own against Rice one-on-one. Couldn’t turn and find the ball but was all over KC’s receiver, who couldn’t reach the ball. The Chiefs kick the FG on 2nd down, and the 1st half is history after Ray Davis returns the kickoff. (Igbinosun: 4 tackles; Harrison Butker: 26-yard FG) Poor 1st half from both offenses. Elements are playing a huge role in the game. Bills’ OL and Cook have made the difference, but the interception in the red zone was a tough pill to swallow. KC’s last drive certainly gives them confidence. 1st half ends with a feeling of a huge missed opportunity by the Bills. I expected more from Josh. (At halftime: Cook, 71 rushing yards; Allen, 5-of-10 for 41 yards; Mahomes, 10-of-15 for 97 yards) 2nd Half KC gets the ball and drives downfield easily. The running and passing game are working flawlessly, and the Bills’ defense has no answer for it. Emmett Johnson finishes the drive rushing for the TD from the 1-yard line. 10-7 Chiefs. (Drive: 7 plays, 56 yards; Johnson: 17 carries, 72 yards, 1 TD) Buffalo’s offense has to answer that now. It’s about time to get something going in the passing game. Josh underthrows Moore badly on 1st down, and it’s almost a fumble on the failed screen pass to Shakir on 2nd down. On 3rd and 10, Josh does his magic, escaping a sack and rushing for the 1st down. His reaction after it, though, is odd. No emotion at all. Weird. (Allen: 7 carries, 43 yards) Next pass by Josh is tipped again, but after it he finds Shakir on 3rd and 7, and then Dalton Kincaid on a screen. (Kincaid: 2 catches on 2 targets, 13 yards) The tush push on 3rd and 1 gets the job done, but then, on 1st down, a crazy INT by Nohl Williams. Shakir drops the screen pass right onto the Chiefs ‘ CB’s arms. Josh’s ball location wasn’t great, but Shakir can’t do that. Another TO in the Red Zone. (Shakir: 3 catches on 6 targets, 33 yards; Bills: 2 turnovers, both in the red zone) Greg “Groot” Rousseau comes to the rescue, sealing another good defensive drive with a sack, his 11th this season. Huge for the Bills that the defense could rebound after two difficult drives. (Rousseau: 3 tackles, 1 sack) Wake up, Josh Allen, it’s time. Promising drive. Bills continue to be able to stay ahead of the chains and to convert 3rd-and-short situations. End of the 3rd as they move past midfield. (Bills: 9-of-16 on 3rd down) 4th quarter is when the Bills’ run game usually makes the difference for the team. If Josh can play decently, the offense should be able to put up points on the board. (Bills: 14 of their 17 first downs came on the ground) 3rd and 3, Josh with the designed run. Holding on the play, and it’s 3rd and 13. Josh escapes the pressure, but his pass is erratic again. Honestly, I can’t remember the last time I’ve been worried about a Josh Allen performance like today. (Allen: 10-of-21 for 81 yards, 0 TD, 2 INT) Bass hits it from 54 yards. Impressive in those conditions. 10-10. Jim Leonhard’s dialing some interesting pressure packages for Mahomes. Here, IGB hits the QB, and Bernard almost intercepts it. (Mahomes: 16-of-29 for 174 yards, 0 TD, 0 INT, 1 sack) Chiefs’ run game is working now, and it opens up the passing game. Thankfully, the refs threw a…
author: Fernando Schmude

title: Bills vs Chiefs: Rashee Rice catch overturned by replay draws criticism from Andy Reid
summary: Late in the Buffalo Bills win over the Kansas City Chiefs, a turning point in the game was decided by replay. On third down inside two minutes, Patrick Mahomes found Rashee Rice over the middle of the field and Rice was popped by Bills safety Amani Hooker. As he fell to the ground, the ball […]
full_text: Nov 26, 2026; Orchard Park, New York, USA; Buffalo Bills defensive back Amani Hooker (22) breaks up a pass intended for Kansas City Chiefs wide receiver Rashee Rice (4) during the fourth quarter at New Highmark Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Gregory Fisher-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Late in the Buffalo Bills win over the Kansas City Chiefs, a turning point in the game was decided by replay. On third down inside two minutes, Patrick Mahomes found Rashee Rice over the middle of the field and Rice was popped by Bills safety Amani Hooker. As he fell to the ground, the ball moved. On the field it was ruled a catch. Because it was inside two minutes, the replay official had to call for a review and not Bills head coach Joe Brady. After replay, it was ruled an incomplete pass. After the game, Chiefs head coach Andy Reid addressed the play, saying he didn’t like the call. “Not one that I agreed with,” said Reid of the replay review. “This came from New York,” Reid said. “They called it a completion. I’m not quite sure what they saw, I saw he had control of the ball, and his elbow hit then the ball hit, but he had control. Normally, in those kind of situations, it has to be clear obvious. To me that was not clear and obvious.” The NBC broadcast spent a lot of time on it during the game and again in the postgame. Rules analyst Terry McAulay thought it was a catch and the Chiefs should have moved the chains. Cris Collinsworth talked about the laces on the ball, and when Rice hit the ground his hand moved down those laces while the ball touched the turf. I think it’s pretty clear the ball moved. I think it’s pretty clear the ball hits the ground. You be the judge: WOW… Refs called this a catch on the field but after review overturned the call and ruled this an incomplete catch for the Chiefs… Very little movement on this ball to overturn that pic.twitter.com/5yZ6sMQqTr — Rate the Refs (@Rate_the_Refs) November 27, 2026

title: Buffalo Bills stock report in insane 13-10 victory vs. Kansas City Chiefs
summary: I picked a bad day to stop sniffing glue. The Buffalo Bills and the Kansas City Chiefs have played plenty of classics over the course of the last decade. It’s been a while since we had a true terrible weather game between these two clubs, and while it might have kept the scoring down from […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - NOVEMBER 26: James Cook III #4 of the Buffalo Bills scores a touchdown in the second quarter against the Kansas City Chiefs at Highmark Stadium on November 26, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Timothy T Ludwig/Getty Images) | Getty Images I picked a bad day to stop sniffing glue. The Buffalo Bills and the Kansas City Chiefs have played plenty of classics over the course of the last decade. It’s been a while since we had a true terrible weather game between these two clubs, and while it might have kept the scoring down from what we would otherwise have expected, the bad weather certainly didn’t lessen the intensity of the game. Buffalo jumped out to a 7-0 lead early, but a red zone turnover kept the Bills from adding to their lead. Kansas City logged their first points in a two-minute drill to close out the first half, and they scored again coming out of the half to give them a 10-7 lead. That score stayed put for a long time. Tyler Bass drilled a 54-yard kick in the fourth quarter to tie. And then, he hit another bomb, this time from 57 yards out, to secure a hard-fought, 13-10 victory. I need a cigarette, and I don’t even smoke. Here are our horns up and horns down for Buffalo from tonight’s game with the Chiefs. _____________________________________________________________________________ Horns Up: Tommy Doman Jr. It’s not often that we can lead with the punter, but in horrendous conditions, Doman and the Buffalo special teams set the tone early. Whereas Kansas City punter Matt Araiza struggled with the weather, uncorking a short punt before he dropped another snap and netted just eight yards on his second attempt, Doman pinned the Chiefs deep with his second attempt, which gave the Bills good field position after they forced a punt. He was also stellar in his other two roles holding on Tyler Bass kicks and performing kickoffs. Doman hit a boomer heading into the two-minute warning in the fourth quarter, pinning the Chiefs at the 13-yard line. It certainly wasn’t perfect, as Doman’s shank just after the two-minute warning in the first half gave the Chiefs solid field position, which led to a Harrison Butker field goal, but he was very good overall in difficult conditions. Horns Up: James Cook III Once again, the offense ran through Cook and the run game. Cook had a touchdown called back after expedited review, and after the Bills were flagged for a false start (with a Kansas City defender in the neutral zone first, but I digress), Cook managed to score the game’s first touchdown anyway. He ran it in from six yards out on second down, giving the Bills an early lead. He even hung onto the first pass thrown by quarterback Josh Allen, as he picked up solid yardage off a play-action pass. Catching passes in normal weather is always nice, but hanging onto one in the conditions each team faced tonight was impressive. Cook was easily the best player on offense for Buffalo, finishing with 32 carries for 117 yards and Buffalo’s lone touchdown, adding one catch for 8 yards as a receiver. Horns Down: The Weather Not exactly a fun set of conditions for tonight’s game, but the Bills came out and did what they needed to do in the early going despite the adverse conditions. With these two teams, it’s never fun to watch a slog in the mud given how explosive the offenses can be. However, if you’re an old-school football person, a little mud helps the aesthetics a bit. I can say that from my couch, but on the field, there’s no doubt in my mind that the players would much rather the clear skies we saw Sunday over the rainy mess we saw tonight. As the game progressed, it became clear that Josh Allen was struggling mightily to throw the football. Patrick Mahomes had his struggles, as well, but Allen really had a difficult time finding the grip and placing the ball where his receivers needed the ball to be. Horns Up: 3-Techs Both Ed Oliver and DeWayne Carter were able to create issues for Chiefs’ left guard Kingsley Suamataia. They each bull-rushed the big guard at times in the first half, flushing Patrick Mahomes from the pocket and drawing holding penalties in the process. Combined with a strong night from other members of the front seven—Greg Rousseau, Bradley Chubb, Deone Walker, and Landon Jackson all made plays—it was nice to see the Bills pressuring Mahomes without needing to blitz. Horns Down: Ball Security I know, I know. The weather was atrocious, so the ball is going to be slick. It’s hard to blame guys for it slipping out of their hands. However, Buffalo had two turnovers in the red zone. That’s a killer against any team. When it’s a team as good as Kansas City? It’s a death sentence. Josh Allen’s first interception came on a tipped ball where it looked like he was targeting Dawson Knox, who was not open in the end zone. Maybe he was trying to throw it away to live another down? Either way, the ball was tipped by George Karlaftis and intercepted in the end zone by Alohi Gilman. Allen’s second interception came when Khalil Shakir mishandled a pass, shoveling it directly into the waiting arms of Nohl Williams. Those plays cost the Bills at least six points. In a messy game, the team that protects the football wins the game. Buffalo made too many mistakes. Horns Up: The Defense What a turnaround for this unit. Do we want to add another caveat to this one? After all, it wasn’t a backup—or third-string—quarterback, but it was horrendous weather. Still, the Buffalo stop unit was up to the task. Buffalo allowed the Chiefs to double-dip, as they scored ten points across their final first-half drive and first second-half drive. The touchdown Buffalo allowed was the first they’d allowed since a sliding grab by Tre Tucker thrown by now-former Las Vegas Raiders quarterback Kirk Cousins back in Week Six. Overall, the Bills looked good against the pass and the run. They held a legit offense to ten points. Greg Rousseau notched his eleventh sack. It was a great night. Horns Down: Jordan Hancock It wasn’t all sunshine and rainbows on the defensive end. Hancock saw a decent amount of time in the slot, and he was beaten on some of the few long passing plays that the Chiefs had. In the first half, he lost Travis Kelce, who secured a big gain. Early in the second half, Hancock had Rashee Rice, and Rice beat him for a first down on a drive where the Chiefs just gashed Buffalo on the way to their first touchdown of the night. Tight end Noah Gray found space on a huge fourth quarter play, as well, where Hancock was the defender and he was screened by his own man. Hancock is a backup-slash-dime player for a reason, but he was a weaker link in an otherwise strong night for the defense. Horns Up: Tyler Bass A 54-yard kick? In this weather? Yeah, Bass stepped up and absolutely nailed it. Trailing 10-7, a miss there would have set the Chiefs up in perfect position to put the game away. Instead, Buffalo’s kicker continued his hot streak and hit an absolute bullet through the uprights to tie the game. Then, with just four seconds remaining, Bass drilled another kick, this time from 57 yards out, to give the Bills the win. What a night, what a season for No. 16. Horns Up: Joe Andreessen A blocked punt on Thanksgiving on National television in front of the home crowd where you grew up?! This is literal fairy-tale stuff. Buffalo’s core special teams group was phenomenal tonight, and Andreessen was the Cool Whip on the chocolate pudding pie. Horns Undecided: You Make the Call Well folks, who did we miss? Let me know in the comments! As for me, I’m going to hang around for a bit, but from the Murphy Family (and the Rumblings Family) to all of you fine people, Happy Thanksgiving!

title: Buffalo Bills OLB Greg Rousseau ties Mario Williams’ team sack total
summary: Buffalo Bills outside linebacker Greg Rousseau moved into a tie for seventh place on the team’s all-time sacks list on Thanksgiving night. Rousseau sacked quarterback Patrick Mahomes on a 3rd & 16 midway through the third quarter on Thanksgiving night to bring his career total to 43, catching former Bills defensive end Mario Williams.  Williams […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - NOVEMBER 26: Patrick Mahomes #15 of the Kansas City Chiefs drops back to pass while being pressured by Greg Rousseau #15 of the Buffalo Bills in the second quarter at Highmark Stadium on November 26, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Joe Hrycych/Getty Images) | Getty Images Buffalo Bills outside linebacker Greg Rousseau moved into a tie for seventh place on the team’s all-time sacks list on Thanksgiving night. Rousseau sacked quarterback Patrick Mahomes on a 3rd & 16 midway through the third quarter on Thanksgiving night to bring his career total to 43, catching former Bills defensive end Mario Williams. Greg Rousseau tallies his 11th sack of the season 💪 KCvsBUF on NBC/Peacock Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/hBKaqwPgjQ — NFL (@NFL) November 27, 2026 Williams spent four seasons (2012-2015) in Buffalo, recording double-digit sacks in each of his first three years with the team. His best season came in 2014 when he recorded 14.5 sacks and earned first-team All-Pro honors. Rousseau, now in his sixth NFL season, has spent his entire career in Buffalo after the Bills selected him with the 30th overall pick in the 2021 NFL Draft. Having already established a new personal single-season record for sacks this year , the 26 year old is now working his way through some familiar names in Buffalo’s history books. Once Rousseau gets past Mario Williams, there’s another Williams waiting for him. Former defensive tackle Kyle Williams (48.5), who spent all 13 of his NFL seasons in Buffalo, sits sixth on the franchise’s all-time list. With six regular-season games remaining, and the way Rousseau has been getting to opposing quarterbacks lately, we might not have to wait until next season to talk about him catching another Williams.

title: Panthers vs Buccaneers: The run game is the big storyline this week
summary: Hello CSR! Happy Black Friday and I hope you all got to enjoy Thanksgiving! I hope the Panthers did too, but didn’t eat too much and are hyped and ready for a pivotal NFC South matchup against the Buccaneers for Monday Night Football. The last time around, the Bucs ran the football down their throats […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NC - NOVEMBER 22: Carolina Panthers outside linebacker Princely Umanmielen (3) and linebacker Devin Lloyd (55) combine for a sack of Baltimore Ravens quarterback Jacoby Brissett (11) during an NFL football game between the Baltimore Ravens and the Carolina Panthers on November 22, 2026 at Bank of America Stadium in Charlotte, N.C. (Photo by John Byrum/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Hello CSR! Happy Black Friday and I hope you all got to enjoy Thanksgiving! I hope the Panthers did too, but didn’t eat too much and are hyped and ready for a pivotal NFC South matchup against the Buccaneers for Monday Night Football. The last time around, the Bucs ran the football down their throats and played excellent defense, en route to a 43-13 win over the Panthers in Charlotte. Now, the Panthers travel to Tampa in what could be a division defining showdown. How do the Panthers stack up? Hopefully, not like last time. The defense has to stop the run The Bucs have been pretty transparent about their offensive gameplay this season; run the football. The Bucs are averaging a whopping 159.6 yards per game which is 1st in the league, and averaging running the ball 51.44% of the time, also 1st in the league. We all know Bucky Irving is good, but they are riding him and Kenneth Gainwell hard this season. The duo has already racked up 1,200 yards between them as Baker Mayfield hasn’t been relied on too heavily as a passer in an injury riddled season. The Panthers defense meanwhile has been a tale of two defenses this season, sometimes giving up 300+ yards on the ground but also shutting down some of the more prominent running backs in guys like Jahmyr Gibbs and Bijan Robinson. Last week, the Panthers did win with many turnovers, but they still allowed 157 yards on the ground for an average of 7.1 yards per carry, and that average was dragged downward by a 13 yard loss on a rush by WR Zay Flowers. There’s not much to be said here, the trenches are going to be the storyline in this game. They have to come out playing fast early on defense. Keep riding Chuba Hubbard on offense The Panthers offense on the other side has settled down from the explosive passing attack they were to start the season. They are still taking the shots down the field, but for the most part they are staying on schedule by getting the ball to Chuba Hubbard, and last week they sprinkled in a healthy mix of Trevor Etienne. The last time these teams met, the two only carried the ball 13 times between the two, and Chuba only carried the rock 7 of those times. The game had gotten out of hand fast, so that was understandable, but that can’t happen again. I do worry about the Buccaneers jumping out ahead early, as the same thing happened last week. The offense can’t start slow this week and allow the Bucs to jump out to a multi-score lead like last week and the first round against the Bucs, because that only favors the Bucs plan of attack. A healthy amount of Chuba Hubbard to start the game should allow the Panthers to get on schedule early. The Bucs’ rushing defense is very good, so this could very well be a challenge, but the offense has to rise to the occasion here. Bonus storyline: Send Princely Umanmielen Last week, the Panthers probably only picked up the win against the Ravens due to their pass rush coming up big in huge passing downs. They didn’t get a ton of pressure consistently, but when they sent Princely opposite of Jaelan Phillips, good things happened. Umanmielen had 1.5 sacks and a tackle for a loss, along with two QB hits. This Buccaneers offensive line is very good, and they’ve kept a beat up Baker Mayfield upright for the most part when he does have to throw. The Panthers can’t let Baker Mayfield scramble like he can to keep drives alive, so I want a healthy Thanksgiving portion of Princely thrown at him. What are you watching for this week, Panthers fans?

title: Reacts Results: Teetering on the edge of the playoffs
summary: The Carolina Panthers get very little respect, both locally and nationally. That is largely because they haven’t earned it. An improved roster and an occasionally clutch quarterback in Bryce Young has yet to translate to a consistently successful team. Hence their 5-5 record. The only thing they really consistently have going for them is that […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NC - OCTOBER 25: Carolina Panthers quarter back Bryce Young (9) fumbles the ball in a pass attempt from a hit by Tampa Bay Buccaneers Payne Durham (87) during an NFL football game between the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and the Carolina Panthers on October 25, 2026 at Bank of America Stadium in Charlotte, N.C. (Photo by John Byrum/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Carolina Panthers get very little respect, both locally and nationally. That is largely because they haven’t earned it. An improved roster and an occasionally clutch quarterback in Bryce Young has yet to translate to a consistently successful team. Hence their 5-5 record. The only thing they really consistently have going for them is that they play in the NFC South. an approximately 0.500 record may be all it takes to win their division while a 10-win NFC North team has the potential to miss the playoffs altogether. The Panthers path to the playoffs is pretty clear, as their chances of making a wildcard berth are virtually non-existent. They need to win the NFC South and, to do that, they really should beat the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Monday Night Football this week. The fun thing is, nobody thinks they can do it. A 5-5 team is heavily favored to lose to a 3-7 team with an injured quarterback by almost every outlet and oddsmaker out there. ESPN gives the Panthers a 32% chance to win and currently predicts that the Bucs will win the division. The Athletic’s playoff simulator barely favors (54%) the Panthers to win the NFC South when looking at the remaining season as a whole. The spread at FanDuel opened favoring the Bucs at home by -2.5 and has shifted to favoring them by -3 Even the Panthers own fans are undecided on if their favorite team can beat the Bucs. Despite that, the math is fairly clear (even if the playoff predictions from major outlets remain opaque). If the Panthers can beat the Bucs—in what should be a very different game all around than their initial Week 7 clash—then their playoff odds skyrocket. ESPN shifts the NFC South to the Panthers just on the results of Monday Night. The Athletic has the Panthers playoff odds jump to 79%. The team is on the cusp of not having to play for the division title every week until the end of the season as they did—and failed to seize—in 2025. That, and the simple high off their Week 11 win against the Baltimore, may explain why fan confidence is still riding relatively high. Health, preparation on a long, holiday week, and the Monday night time slot will all have a hand in how this week turns out. One thing seems certain, however, with the stakes high and revenge on their minds, the Panthers seem unlikely to overlook the Bucs a second time.

summary: In the first quarter of yesterday’s game in Detroit, Chicago Bears tight end Colston Loveland was injured when he was rolled up from behind. The Bears called it a knee injury, and he was carted off the field, frustrated and in tears. Today’s news is much more optimistic, as ESPN’s Courtnet Cronin wrote, “Per league […]
full_text: DETROIT,MICHIGAN-NOVEMBER 26:Chicago Bears tight end Colston Loveland is carted off of the field due to an injury during an NFL football game between the Chicago Bears and the Detroit Lions in Detroit, Michigan USA, on Thursday, November 26, 2026. (Photo by Amy Lemus/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images In the first quarter of yesterday’s game in Detroit, Chicago Bears tight end Colston Loveland was injured when he was rolled up from behind. The Bears called it a knee injury, and he was carted off the field, frustrated and in tears. Today’s news is much more optimistic, as ESPN’s Courtnet Cronin wrote, “Per league source, Bears tight end Colston Loveland is considered week-to-week with the left knee injury. He will get a second opinion soon, but no determination on whether he is an IR candidate has been made.” Cronin’s report came about a half hour after ESPN’s Adam Schefter also shared positive news about Loveland: “There still is additional testing to be done, but the current belief is that Loveland could return later this season.” Schefter’s initial report also included that an injured reserve stint was expected, which would mean Loveland would be out a minimum of four games, but he followed up with a report that corroborated Cornin’s: “Until Colston Loveland gets a second opinion on his knee injury, the Bears are not making any decisions about injured reserve, and he will be considered a week-to-week until then.” There are six games remaining in the regular season, so in the best-case scenario, we will see Colston again. In the meantime, the Bears have two active tight ends on the 53-man roster, Sam Roush and Stephen Carlson, and they have 26-year-old Qadir Ismail (6’6″, 232) on the practice squad. Earlier today, the Chicago Tribune’s Brad Biggs reported that defensive lineman Dayo Odeyingbo underwent surgery and won’t return this season. Odeyingbo injured his quad in Week 5 and was in the midst of a solid 2026, with 9 tackles, 3 tackles for loss, 3 sacks, and 2 passes defended while playing up and down Chicago’s defensive line. For those curious, Dayo has one more year left on his contract, and his 2027 cap hit would be $26,500,000. If cut, there would be $11,500,000 in dead money.

title: Bears vs. Lions: Inside the Snap Counts, Stats, and the Return of the Cardiac Bears
summary: The Chicago Bears came back and won six games a season ago and earned the nickname “Cardiac Bears,” but so far this season they haven’t needed much drama to win. In their previous five games, the Bears never trailed, though they needed a last-second field goal to beat the Buccaneers a few weeks ago after […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 26: Caleb Williams #18 of the Chicago Bears scores a two-point conversion during the fourth quarter of an NFL football game against the Detroit Lions at Ford Field on November 26, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Chicago Bears came back and won six games a season ago and earned the nickname “Cardiac Bears,” but so far this season they haven’t needed much drama to win. In their previous five games, the Bears never trailed, though they needed a last-second field goal to beat the Buccaneers a few weeks ago after the Bucs tied it late. But yesterday, the drama returned as the Bears fell behind early to the Detroit Lions and didn’t take a lead until Caleb Williams hit Rome Odunze for a 6-yard touchdown with just three seconds left. The extra point was good, making it 39 to 35, and Detroit’s final Stanford Band play couldn’t get it done. The Bears won and gave us the happiest Thanksgiving ever, while Ben Johnson hit the final Stanky Leg from Motown. The Lions have a fantastic offense, and the 549 yards they put up on the Bears is their most since November 17, 2024, when they put up 645 on the Jaguars. Detroit’s Jahmyr Gibbs continued his push for league MVP with 21 carries for 205 yards (9.8) and 3 touchdowns, and 5 receptions for 47 yards. The Bears offense racked up 458 yards, got 27 first downs (the Lions had 27 too), and went 7-for-14 on third downs, and 2-for-3 on fourth downs. Chicago’s defense struggled most of the day, but they got their only takeaway in the fourth quarter on an interception by Dillon Thieneman. On Detroit’s next series, T.J. Edwards got a huge fourth-down tackle on Gibbs. The Lions went 1-for-2 on fourth-down attempts and 4-for-12 (33.3%) on third down. Let’s look at the Bears’ playing-time breakdown and a few individual stats from the game. OFFENSE Caleb Williams was solid all afternoon, but in the fourth quarter he went 13-for-20 for 135 yards, 2 TDs, and a passer rating of 117.7. He added two runs for 10 yards and a 2-point conversion. We haven’t seen him much this year, but it’s fun to see the Iceman again. Rome Odunze had 5 receptions for 78 yards and both TDs in the fourth quarter. I wonder if Ben Johnson and his coaching staff picked up on something while watching film, because Next Gen Stats says Williams “completed 10 of 11 passes targeting flat routes for 127 yards, the most in any game since at least 2018.” Today marked Caleb Williams’ 8th career win when trailing in the final 2 minutes of regulation. That is the most by a starting quarterback in their first 3 seasons since the 1970 merger. The next closest QB is Ben Roethlisberger with 6. @ESPNInsights — Courtney Cronin (@CourtneyRCronin) November 26, 2026 DEFENSE Dillon Thieneman picked up his team-leading third interception. James Lynch’s 2 tackles for loss are a career high. Jeffery Simmons didn’t have the same statistical impact as his previous three games, but his presence was felt when the Lions kept jumping offsides. Detroit cried cheater, but the refs didn’t see it that way. In the fourth quarter, T.J. Edwards tipped the pass that led to Thieneman’s pick, and he had 3 tackles. Cornerback Tyrique Stevenson, who was active but questionable with a groin issue, did not play. SPECIAL TEAMS* *The above image has players who only played in the third phase. Cairo Santos was perfect on the day with a 40-yard field goal and all 4 extra points. Tory Taylor had 2 punts for 90 yards (45.0 net average), and both were inside the 20. Daniel Hardy had 3 special teams tackles, and D. Marco Jackson had 2. To check out the complete Bears vs. Lions box score, I find ESPN’s site is easy to navigate. All statistics and snap counts, as well as the accompanying pictures, are taken directly from the NFL’s Game Statistic and Information System.

title: 10 Bears Takes: Superman is back, a 9-2 start, and more on the last-second win
summary: The Thanksgiving opener might have started a bit slowly, but the second half gave football fans everything and more to kick off an action-packed Turkey Day. Coming into the game, the Chicago Bears had not trailed in five complete games. That streak ended early, and they ultimately flipped the script, leading for only three seconds. […]
full_text: Chicago Bears wide receiver Rome Odunze catches a touchdown pass in the end zone with three seconds left against the Detroit Lions on Thursday, Nov. 26, 2026, at Ford Field in Detroit, Mich. The Bears won 39-35. (Stacey Wescott/Chicago Tribune/Tribune News Service via Getty Images) The Thanksgiving opener might have started a bit slowly, but the second half gave football fans everything and more to kick off an action-packed Turkey Day. Coming into the game, the Chicago Bears had not trailed in five complete games. That streak ended early, and they ultimately flipped the script, leading for only three seconds. In the end, quarterback Caleb Williams put on his Superman cape and led the Bears to another comeback win. At 9-2, Chicago is in the driver’s seat for a playoff spot and controls their own destiny when it comes to winning the division. That said, there was plenty to dissect on Thursday, including a key injury and some concerning trends. We’ll dive into all of that and more in our Week 12 installment of 10 Bears Takes. 1. With their win on Thursday afternoon, Ben Johnson becomes the first head coach to have back-to-back winning seasons since Lovie Smith, exactly two decades ago. Just as important for team morale, Johnson finally got the monkey off his back while earning his first win against his former team. Unlike last season, 2026 has been a much smoother ride for the Bears, with more leads and more wins. Outside of them blowing a big lead against Tampa Bay, quarterback Caleb Williams has not had many chances to lead fourth-quarter comebacks. Thursday’s game didn’t start promising, and every time it felt like the Bears were about to recapture momentum, their offense would stall, or their defense couldn’t get a stop. Frankly, there were many times that it felt like Chicago was down and out of the game. Instead of crumbling and allowing the game to get out of hand, they kept swinging back, and with the game on the line on a third-and-goal from the Lions’ six-yard line, Williams found Rome Odunze in the back of the end zone for the game-winning touchdown with just three seconds to go. Since taking over as the team’s head coach last season, Johnson is now 20-8 in just over a season and a half in Chicago. His .714 win percentage currently ranks 1st of all 19 head coaches in franchise history. Thursday’s win allowed him to overtake Ralph Jones’ position at the top (.706). Despite that, he’s won just three divisional games over 10 tries. Not only had Johnson failed to beat Detroit in his first two attempts, but Williams also came into Thursday with a 0-4 record, despite two close games that didn’t go his way. Through his first 28 games as the team’s head coach, Johnson has done a great job of breaking down old barriers that have held them back since the Mike Ditka days. The latest of which was clinching back-to-back winning seasons for the first time in exactly 20 years. Even more impressive is the fact that wins didn’t start coming in bunches for Lovie and company until his second year as the team’s head coach. The job is still far from complete, and their divisional record needs to keep improving, but considering the Bears were close to a 50-50 bet even to make the playoffs, Year 2 under Johnson has gone about as well as possible. It’s also worth noting that their current six-game winning streak is the longest they’ve experienced since they opened up the season at 6-0 in 2006. Like it or not, there are many parallels between what the Bears are doing now and the 2005-2006 team led by Smith. 2. The loss of tight end Colston Loveland is a tough one, especially after Cole Kmet went down earlier in the year. While the initial hope (via David J. Chao) is that it’s an MCL sprain that might cost him a short-term stint on Injured Reserve, the ultimate hope (and goal) is that he’ll be back for the end of the season and into the playoffs. Even if he beats that timeline and returns after four games on IR, it’s a big blow for a team that has already lost Kmet for the year to a torn ACL. Loveland has had an up-and-down sophomore season, but his target share and overall involvement in the offense have picked up in recent weeks. Holding onto the ball has been an issue at times this year, but even when he wasn’t a factor in the receiving game, he was the team’s best blocker with Kmet on the shelf. At least in the short term, the Bears will look to third-round rookie Sam Roush and journeyman tight end Stephen Carlson. Unfortunately for Chicago, the trade deadline has already passed, so any help that might be coming from an outside source will have to be in the form of a street free agent. It’s possible that the team could elevate Quadir Ismail before next weekend’s game, but one thing is for sure: What was once a strength is going to be something that Johnson and his coaching staff are going to have to scheme around. Speaking of scheming around, it seems safe to assume that the Bears will feature more 11 personnel. Luther Burden and Odunze have taken turns being the featured receiver in this offense, and with veteran Kalif Raymond and third-round rookie Zavion Thomas ready to step into bigger roles, there should be confidence that Johnson can keep this offense moving in the right direction. This could also open up more opportunities for former undrafted free agent Jahdae Walker, although his “drop” on Thursday in a big spot was not his best moment. We should find out more in the coming days on the long-term prognosis of Loveland, but assuming that Loveland isn’t lost for the year, the offensive staff will need to get creative by reimagining their passing offense. 3. Despite two short weeks already behind them, the Bears will still have two more over their final six games of the season. When the Bears are good, the NFL loves it. Last year was somewhat of a test run for Ben Johnson and company, but now that they have proven themselves as a good, fun team to watch, the NFL has maximized opportunities to get them in standalone games. That has led to multiple short (and long) weeks. Thanksgiving marked the second time they’ve played on Thursday this season, and even if they don’t get that short a week again to finish out the season, they’ll play a Saturday game against Buffalo, followed by a Christmas Day game the following week. Some might see this as a negative, and to a certain extent, it is. Luckily, the Bears had a relatively late bye, and despite a short week heading into Detroit, they’ll have another mini bye to make more adjustments for the final six games of the season. That said, playing back-to-back games with one less day of rest is not ideal, especially with a divisional race that is shaping up to go all the way down to the wire. The good news is that Ben Johnson is now 7-2 coming off short weeks, so his track record for having his team prepared is extremely promising. That said, facing the Bills and Packers on short weeks isn’t ideal. It is worth mentioning that both of their opponents will be experiencing the same shortened preparation period. With just six games remaining in the regular season and hopes of a deep playoff run into late January or early February, the Bears are just a few short weeks away from some added adversity that fans should have confidence they’ll be prepared for. Moving forward into next season and beyond, hopefully they won’t draw the short end of the stick when it comes to abbreviated weeks quite as often. 4. Over the last few weeks, the offense had taken a noticeable step back. Between poor offensive line play and a gun-shy quarterback, the second half was a welcome development. When Williams first returned, the offense looked unstoppable. The running game wasn’t nearly as effective, but the passing game attacked defenses from multiple directions. Their 34-point performance against an elite Seattle defense felt like a statement, and after they jumped out to a 17-point lead against the Buccaneers, it felt like this group was…

title: The Chicago Bears are on top of the world
summary: Down by 11 points with less than eight minutes to go in the fourth quarter, the Chicago Bears had their backs against the wall in their Thanksgiving showdown against the Detroit Lions on Thursday. But somehow, someway, they found a way to win, such has been the case for much of Ben Johnson’s tenure as […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 26: Caleb Williams #18 of the Chicago Bears warms up prior to an NFL football game against the Detroit Lions at Ford Field on November 26, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images Down by 11 points with less than eight minutes to go in the fourth quarter, the Chicago Bears had their backs against the wall in their Thanksgiving showdown against the Detroit Lions on Thursday. But somehow, someway, they found a way to win, such has been the case for much of Ben Johnson’s tenure as their head coach. Thanks to a last-second touchdown pass from Caleb Williams to Rome Odunze, the Bears picked up the 39-35 win over the Lions, marking their sixth win in a row and improving their record to 9-2 for the year. They were in search of their first divisional win of the year, and after falling in each of their first two NFC North games, they came away with a massive win, granting them sole possession of first place in the division. In between bites of turkey and second helpings of mashed potatoes, Bears fans had plenty to be thankful for watching this game. Here are some of my takeaways from Thursday’s victory. Offensive execution at its finest They don’t call him “Iceman” for nothing. Caleb Williams was lights out in the fourth quarter, throwing for 135 passing yards and two touchdowns in the final stretch for the Bears. Both of his touchdown passes ended up going to Rome Odunze, who himself deserves significant credit for his toe-tapping touchdown grab in the back corner of the end zone. The Bears’ offense climbed out of the hole it made for itself and utterly dominated down the stretch, controlling the last stretch of the game. Chicago utilized a pass-heavy approach on Thursday, and that worked out well for them. Odunze finished the game with six catches for 87 yards, on top of his aforementioned two touchdowns. D’Andre Swift added seven catches for 95 yards, on top of his 65 rushing yards and a touchdown on nine carries. When Colston Loveland went down with an injury, the likes of Sam Roush and Stephen Carlson contributed with a few plays. Luther Burden III had an impressive 25-yard gain, to boot. The Bears have such a deep arsenal of weapons in the passing game, and though the absences of Loveland and Cole Kmet loom large, head coach Ben Johnson did a great job of adjusting, and his players stepped up when it mattered most. Room for improvement Of course, no game in the NFL is ever going to be perfect. For the Bears to have been trailing by 11 points to begin with, they had to have made some mistakes. Ball security remains an issue, as both Loveland and Williams turned the ball over with fumbles, with the latter’s fumble resulting in a safety to add to the Lions’ lead. Offensively, the run game was inconsistent, as D’Andre Swift’s occasional big run was dragged down by a poor offensive line performance and Kyle Monangai’s inefficiency, having tallied just 1.9 yards per carry on Thursday, despite rushing for two touchdowns. As the scoreboard would indicate, Chicago’s defense had some issues against the Lions. Detroit has an elite offense — it ranks No. 3 in the NFL with an 88.4 PFN Offense Impact grade — but the Bears had some discouraging lapses on Thursday. The defensive line failed to generate pressure on a consistent basis, and even with Jeffery Simmons often being double-teamed or schemed around, the rest of the defensive line couldn’t throw Jared Goff off his rhythm much. The cornerbacks got beat in coverage a handful of times, and Jahmyr Gibbs managed to run for 205 yards and three touchdowns. That’s never a great day at the office. Obviously, there’s much more positive to take from a win like this than there is negative. Rather than lamenting the weaknesses, I like to think of these as reasons why Chicago hasn’t even reached its ceiling yet, and considering how good they already are, that’s a scary thought for the rest of the NFL. The Bears have the right group in place I feel confident in saying that the Bears currently have their core in place. I also feel confident in saying that this core has an extremely high ceiling that could end in this team winning the Super Bowl. Maybe that will be this year, maybe it will come in a different year, and maybe it won’t come at all. But there’s so much to like about this team. They have their franchise quarterback, one of the best head coaches in the NFL, and a deep group of weapons in the passing game. Chicago also has superstar players at positions like offensive tackle and defensive tackle, and its defense has shown that it can step up when it matters most and still generate turnovers at a high level. The Bears have now beaten several top teams across the NFL. They defeated each of last year’s Super Bowl competitors in back-to-back weeks, notably marching into Seattle to beat the Seahawks in a difficult road environment. Their win on Thursday against the Lions might’ve been the most impressive of them all, because it looked like they were being outplayed by one of the NFL’s best teams, but they found a way to pull it all together and achieve the comeback victory. That’s a testament to the Bears’ coaching staff and the heart that this current roster brings to the table. Time will tell how far this Bears team ends up going. But I believe that the primary pieces are in place for this group to do some special things.

title: Bears and Lions Go Blow for Blow, but Bears take the Turkey Home!
summary: Bears vs. Lions for First Place Ford Field on Thanksgiving delivered the NFC North heavyweight fight the records promised—two 8-2 teams with first place on the line—and Detroit left the first half with the clearer edge – mostly due to costly mistakes and some bad ball luck. The Lions controlled the early minutes, absorbed Chicago’s […]
full_text: Sep 14, 2025; Detroit, Michigan, USA; Chicago Bears quarterback Caleb Williams (18) passes the ball against the Detroit Lions during the first quarter of the game at Ford Field. Mandatory Credit: Lon Horwedel-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Bears vs. Lions for First Place Ford Field on Thanksgiving delivered the NFC North heavyweight fight the records promised—two 8-2 teams with first place on the line—and Detroit left the first half with the clearer edge – mostly due to costly mistakes and some bad ball luck. The Lions controlled the early minutes, absorbed Chicago’s response, then took advantage of a late Bears mistake to build a nine-point lead heading into the break. And then that beautiful, beautiful second half! 1st Quarter Detroit took the ball first and moved it efficiently. Gibbs found early running room, and St. Brown made a one-handed catch that put the Lions inside the 10. The Bears stiffened near the goal line, forcing Campbell to take the points on Jake Bates’ 24-yard field goal. Lions 3-0. Chicago answered with a promising drive that reached the red zone before Derrick Moore punched the ball out of Colston Loveland’s hands. Detroit recovered. One possession later, Loveland got rolled up while blocking and was carted off with a knee injury. He’s done for the day. Already without Cole Kmet, the Bears are down to Sam Roush and Stephen Carlson at tight end. Detroit used the field position to keep the pressure on and finished the quarter driving deep into Chicago territory. Gooch Hot Take: The Loveland sequence was a double gut-punch—fumble killed a drive, and his injury removes one of Caleb’s most reliable targets. That’s the kind of early self-inflicted damage that usually travels in a rivalry game on the road. Detroit didn’t have to be perfect, though Goff was close to it for most of the half. They just needed Chicago to hand them extra opportunities, and the Bears provided them. 2nd Quarter Detroit finished the long drive with Gibbs’ 1-yard touchdown run. Bates converted. Lions 10-0. Chicago responded with Salvon Ahmed’s 46-yard run that flipped the field, but the Lions’ defense held them to a Cairo Santos 40-yard field goal. 10-3. Williams and the offense found another gear on the next possession. A 33-yard catch-and-run by D’Andre Swift set up short-yardage work, and Kyle Monangai punched it in from a yard out. Santos’ extra point tied it at 10-10 with just over four minutes left. Detroit got the ball back, moved it some with St. Brown, then punted. Chicago had a chance to take the lead in the two-minute drill, but Williams was sacked deep in his own territory. On the ensuing pla,y he was strip-sacked; the Lions recovered, but an illegal batting penalty on the Bears gave Detroit the choice of the ball at the 10 or the safety. Campbell took the points and the ball. 12-10 Lions. Detroit then drove again. After overcoming a couple of false starts, Goff hit Jameson Williams on a deep corner route into the red zone. With time winding down, Goff found Sam LaPorta in the end zone for the touchdown. 19-10 Lions at the half. Gooch Hot Take: The safety was the turning point that didn’t need to happen. Chicago had just tied the game and had the ball with a chance to go into the break even or ahead. Instead, a deep sack, a strip, and a penalty turned a competitive half into a nine-point deficit. The LaPorta score was the exclamation point—Detroit took the free points, got the ball back, and finished the drive. That’s the difference between a team that manages late situations and one that creates them. Gooch Halftime Thoughts Lions 19, Bears 10 is a bigger hole than the overall play suggests, but the path to get there was real. Detroit controlled the first 20 minutes with better field position, a physical run game from Gibbs, and the benefit of Chicago’s early mistakes. The Bears showed they can answer—explosive plays from Ahmed and Swift, a red-zone finish from Monangai—but they did it while playing short-handed at tight end and after spotting the Lions free possessions and a safety. Williams has been clean on interceptions so far, which matters after the four-pick night against Tampa, but the margin for error is thinner without Loveland and after the late-half penalty. The second half would turn on whether Chicago could sustain drives without their tight end, who was becoming the go-to target, and whether the Bears’ front could keep Gibbs and the Detroit run game from grinding out another long possession. Detroit has the better track record of closing these kinds of games at home. Chicago has the Caleb. At the half the Lions have the clearer path, but the team that stops handing the other one extra chances will decide whether this stays a one-score game or turns into a Thanksgiving statement. 3rd Quarter Chicago came out of the break needing a response and got one. Kyle Monangai’s second 1-yard touchdown of the afternoon cut the lead to 19-17. Detroit answered with Jahmyr Gibbs’ second short-yardage score of the day to push it back to 26-17. The Bears kept coming. D’Andre Swift broke a 30-yard run for the score that made it 26-24 with just over three minutes left in the quarter. Two possessions, two touchdowns, and the game was back to a one-score affair after looking like it might get away. Gooch Hot Take: The third quarter was the moment the Bears stopped playing like a team that had spotted Detroit free points and started playing like a team that still believed the scoreboard was temporary. Swift’s 30-yarder was the kind of explosive run that changes the energy in a building that had been tilted Detroit’s way since the safety. 4th Quarter Detroit briefly regained control. Jake Bates’ 40-yard field goal made it 29-24. Then Gibbs ripped off a 70-yard touchdown run—his third score of the day—though the extra point was missed, leaving it 35-24. That looked like the dagger. It wasn’t. Caleb Williams hit Rome Odunze for a 41-yard touchdown, then ran in the two-point conversion himself to pull within three at 35-32. With the game on the line, Williams drove the Bears down the field one last time and found Odunze again, this time from six yards out, with three seconds left. The score made it 39-35. No extra point was needed. Gooch Hot Take: The 70-yard Gibbs run felt like the play that should have ended it. Detroit had the lead, the building, and the momentum. Chicago answered with two straight touchdown drives, including a two-point conversion that kept them alive and a final drive that finished the job. That’s the difference between a good team that can get ahead and a team that can close when the margin is thin and the clock is running.
