title: Thanksgiving NFL football had it all: Comebacks, walk-offs and plenty of points
summary: Three go-ahead scores in the final minute? Two comebacks from double-digit deficits? And 174 combined points across the three games? Yeah, Thursday was awesome.
full_text:
That was the best day of Thanksgiving football in my living memory.

 To be fair, my living memory is not that long. As a proud Gen Zer, my earliest Thanksgiving football memory is watching Peyton Manning throw six touchdown passes against the Joey Harrington-led Lions in 2004. (I was at my aunt's house, and later that night, I watched "The Empire Strikes Back" for the first time with my cousins. Core memory.) But I don't think a three-game sequence can get better than what we saw Thursday.

 Bears-Lions was decided with three seconds left on the clock, with Chicago winning 39-35 . Eagles-Cowboys was decided with two seconds left on the clock, with Philadelphia winning 39-38 . And Chiefs-Bills was decided as time expired, with Buffalo winning 13-10 . According to Elias Sports Bureau, this Thanksgiving was the first day in NFL history -- regular or postseason -- in which every game had a go-ahead score in the final minute of the fourth quarter (minimum three games played).

 Much as a Thanksgiving plate has something for everyone, the 2026 Thanksgiving games were all enjoyable -- but they came with three distinct flavors.

 The opening game at Ford Field was electric . Bears quarterback Caleb Williams and Lions running back Jahmyr Gibbs took the field with the NFC North lead on the line, and they did what they always do: broke physics and defied mortality. Gibbs ripped off a 70-yard touchdown run in which he almost hit 22 mph, per NFL Next Gen Stats. It was one of three scores for Gibbs on the day, and it was his second game this season with at least 250 scrimmage yards.

 Ah, hang on. It was his second game in the past three weeks with at least 250 scrimmage yards. He is the only player to ever do that.

 Yet the Lions lost. They lost a game in which their running back ran for over 200 yards, which no team had done since 2013. The loss came down not to one play, but to 14 different butterfly moments across an excruciating fourth quarter. The missed extra point after a taunting penalty on the Gibbs 70-yarder. The tipped interception off the hand of both Bears linebacker  T.J. Edwards and Lions receiver  Jameson Williams . Tight end  Brock Wright 's drop. Another taunting penalty later in the quarter after a heroic pass breakup from safety  Kerby Joseph . The fourth-down tackle of Gibbs by Edwards again (after an aggressive decision by Detroit coach Dan Campbell).

 And of course, the touchdown pass to receiver  Rome Odunze .

 

 This was a clean pocket and a pristine look. Watch Williams calmly feather this ball in there -- all touch, no laser beam -- while still ensuring it arrives before Odunze runs himself out of bounds. By a blade of grass, he pulled it off.

 Does any franchise have a greater grip on the national attention when it is playing than Chicago? When the football is on, who pins you to the couch like these Bears, who have won four games since the start of last season in which they trailed in the fourth quarter by at least 10 points?

 If the Bears' last-second win over the Lions induced heart palpitations, Eagles-Cowboys induced belly laughter. Everything in this game was ridiculous. Over the course of the game, Cowboys wide receiver George Pickens achieved the following:

 
 Dropped a walk-in 63-yard touchdown 
 Converted a third-and-16 by snatching the ball off a defender's back 
 Lost 12 yards after the catch on a would-be third-down conversion, which is the most negative YAC on a play (excluding laterals) in at least the past two decades 
 Threw a designed cross-field lateral with arc so that it ended up as an illegal forward pass 
 Caught a 15-yard pass to set up what should have been the game-sealing field goal 
 
 Pickens' play was, somehow, not the most amusing or astonishing of the game. Those honors belong to Eagles quarterback Joe Milton -- who was on the Cowboys' practice squad just two months ago -- for the single most jaw-dropping display of arm talent I have ever seen on a football field.

 According to Next Gen Stats, Milton had two throws that went a whopping 64.4 yards by air distance -- yes, two separate throws that traveled the exact same impossibly long distance. One of them was this DeVonta Smith touchdown.

 

 You will notice that Milton does not need to hitch into this 64.4-yard throw. That is because he is a wizard, perhaps, or a time traveler from a future era of nanorobotic biological enhancements.

 If football were purely an entertainment product with no championships, no billions of dollars of investment on the line, every game would look like Milton's outing Thursday. Deep balls on deep balls. I couldn't blink for fear of missing another shot. It was like watching  Steph Curry  in the 3-point contest. Majesty at distance.

 Of Milton's 311 passing yards, 276 (88.7%) came through air yards; only 35 came after the catch. Since 1992 -- as far back as ESPN Research can take us -- this is the only game of at least 300 passing yards with 40 or fewer yards after the catch. That should not be a surprise, because this is not how football has ever worked on the material plane. Milton threw so far downfield and so fearlessly into the sideline that receivers were either basically out of bounds or already in the end zone upon the ball's arrival. The middle of the field, where the entire modern game is played, is for mortal men. What is a checkdown to someone with this kind of arm?

 

 On the other side, these 2026 Cowboys are a particularly compelling team to watch lose given the spectacular scale of their collapses. The 5-7 Cowboys had a 99.4% win probability at the peak of this game, per ESPN's model. They let a listless Eagles team that had not scored more than 22 points in a game since Week 2 score 22 points in the fourth quarter alone . This was the second home game the Cowboys have lost this season in which they led by at least 14 points in the fourth quarter (the other being the Week 8 loss to Arizona ). According to the Elias Sport Bureau, they are the only team to achieve that feat in a season in NFL history.

 Bears-Lions was electric. Eagles-Cowboys was absurd. With the table so nicely set and the bird so wonderfully cooked, how could Chiefs-Bills not be uproarious? Instead, it was a cold shower.

 For four quarters, arguably the two greatest quarterbacks alive played in gusts of wind and sheets of rain. Patrick Mahomes mishandled multiple snaps. Josh Allen had 88 passing yards and threw two picks in the red zone -- both tipped. Chiefs punter Matt Araiza dropped a snap and saw another punt blocked. Chiefs kicker Harrison Butker missed a critical field goal, but we can't blame that one fully on the weather. Bills kicker Tyler Bass nailed two 54-plus-yard field goals in the fourth quarter to tie it then win it. No other player in NFL history hit that exact sequence of kicks -- first to tie, then to win, both of at least 54 yards -- in one fourth quarter ever before.

 After two high-scoring games, it's easy to christen the third a sobering disappointment. I disagree. Yes, Mahomes and Allen typically treat us to more explosive affairs. But football is a grimy sport as much as it is a dazzling one, and that tough underbelly must be honored on Thanksgiving just the same. Forgotten behind the 70-yard Gibbs touchdown is his 1-yard score in the second quarter in which a Bears safety bounced off him like he was made of steel. Forgotten behind Milton's deep ball are the run stuffs by the Eagles' defense that got the offense the ball back to win the game. Not all NFL games are as fun or as shocking as Eagles-Cowboys or Bears-Lions. But every game is, at its core, what Chiefs-Bills was in its entirety: physical, ugly, agonizing and all about execution.

 To watch Mahomes and Allen mud-wrestle Thursday night and feel robbed of greatness is to misapprehend greatness. In sports, greatness is across time. It cannot be achieved in one season or game, let alone one play. And it cannot be achieved only in glittering…

title: Playoff hero Patrick Jeffers is now in the ESPN fantasy football Hall of Fame
summary: For five weeks at the end of 1999, Patrick Jeffers was was a fantasy football league winner, highlighted by a 33-point effort in Week 16.
full_text:
Fantasy football is all about fun, competition and camaraderie, but it's also another way to appreciate the best of the best in the NFL. For more than three decades, ESPN Fantasy has been here with you, celebrating peak performers and magical moments.

 Presenting the ESPN Fantasy Football Hall of Fame   , which honors the best players and acknowledges the most memorable moments since the advent of our game in 1995, the first year fantasy football was available on ESPN.com. 

 Take me to the ESPN Fantasy Football Hall of Fame 
 Class of 2026 Week 12 Inductee: Patrick Jeffers' 33-point game 

 Dec. 26, 1999 (Week 16) 
 33.0 fantasy points 
 5 receptions, 160 receiving yards, 2 receiving TDs 

 Jeffers is the quintessential example of both an NFL one-year wonder and a fantasy football playoff hero. A fifth-round pick in 1996 playing for his third organization in four seasons, Jeffers stepped into the Panthers' starting lineup midseason and wound up scoring the third-most fantasy points among wide receivers over the final 12 weeks of the 1999 season. It was the fantasy playoffs, however, where Jeffers truly shined brightest. Five of his six career games with 20-plus fantasy points came in the final five weeks of 1999, and he scored 33.0 in this game that counted the most, as it was a title week in fantasy leagues.

 

 Jeffers will be inducted Sunday during " Fantasy Focus Countdown " (10 a.m. ET on ESPN2). Tune in each week through Week 16 as we reveal all 18 members of the inaugural class of the ESPN Fantasy Football Hall of Fame.

title: Best friends Pat Surtain II, Jaylen Waddle ecstatic about reuniting on Broncos
summary: Surtain and Waddle bonded immediately at Alabama six years ago and have embraced the chance to play together again in Denver on a team with Super Bowl hopes.
full_text:
ENGLEWOOD, Colo. -- Karl Scott still laughs at the memory, the moment when he knew Denver Broncos cornerback Pat Surtain II and wide receiver Jaylen Waddle were destined to be best friends.

 It was at a Tuscaloosa, Alabama, bowling alley on a blistering summer afternoon in 2018 during what Scott, who was the Alabama defensive backs coach at the time, described as a team-building event for the Crimson Tide's incoming recruiting class. Surtain and Waddle were among Alabama's newly minted freshmen, and their bond already stood out to the coach.

 "They weren't going to be just guys who happened to be on the same team. They were going to be the guy who's got your back for each other," said Scott, now the  Seattle Seahawks ' secondary coach and defensive passing game coordinator. "Frick and Frack, man, just Frick and Frack. There wasn't a time I didn't see them together."

 A wide smile crept across Surtain's face after a recent Broncos practice when recalling that day, with the All-Pro calling it "just the beginning of it all."

 

 The Broncos are nearly two-thirds through the 2026 season, the first that Waddle and Surtain have spent as teammates since playing together on Alabama's 2020 College Football Playoff championship team. They were reunited when the Broncos acquired Waddle from the Miami Dolphins this past offseason for first- and third-round draft picks along with a fourth-round pick swap. And when the 8-2 Broncos play at the 6-4 Pittsburgh Steelers on Friday in Acrisure Stadium ( 3 p.m. ET, Prime Video ), it will be the sixth time Surtain and Waddle have taken the field together not only as NFL teammates, but also close friends.

 Not we-play-for-the-same-team friends. Best friends.

 "I think we know it doesn't happen that way very much -- you don't expect to be able to get a job where your best friend is, at least in this league," said Waddle, who leads the Broncos with 33 receptions for 398 receiving yards and two touchdowns this season. "I don't know why, we just hit it off right away, immediate, and it's just kept on."

 
 'We just developed that friendship' 
 Surtain was the  cornerback prospect of the 2018 recruiting class, a 6-foot-2, 200-pound five-star player whose father, Patrick Surtain, played for a decade in the NFL.

 Scott said the pursuit of Surtain was considered the "feast on the table" and that then-Crimson Tide coach Nick Saban believed Surtain to be one of the most polished, talented incoming freshmen he had ever seen at the position.

 "And Pat was in the front row, always, and sat right next to Nick -- always," Scott said. "A savant, there's a bunch of everything in there, bunch of personality, bunch of intelligence, bunch of determination, bunch of work. Everything. He is just not going to show it to you on his face."

 Antarctica has nothing on Surtain, who goes beyond straight-up cool. Then there is Waddle, a 5-foot-10, 185-pound ball of energy, a player who seems to have the launch sequence permanently activated. He was a top recruit in his own right, a four-star player out of Bellaire, Texas.

 Surtain said they had interacted some on the recruiting trail but that they really bonded right away after arriving in Tuscaloosa.

 "We just developed that friendship. You become roommates, we're best friends, and I think [Waddle] just saw me sooner a little bit," Surtain said. "Everybody thought I was one of those kids who was a five-star coming in, you know, over my head a little bit, thinking I was all that. But I think they realized pretty quick I wasn't like that, that maybe I was pretty cool and regular [laughs]. But Jaylen, I felt like, knew me.

 "He's got jokes all day. But right from the start I was like 'I've known him my whole life.'"

 But there weren't many jokes on the field in practice, when the two would go head to head in drills. It was all business. They wanted to beat each other, and honed each other's skill sets in pursuit of that goal.

 

 "I'd stand there in practice -- you're talking about a group I had with Xavier McKinney , Trevon Diggs , and Pat's out there with the [first team] as a true freshman -- and I'd watch Pat and Jaylen just go at it, almost ruthless with each other," Scott said. "Just pushing it all the time, and then play's over, practice is over, they were those guys again. They didn't let competition injure that bond. It was part of it."

 Surtain and Waddle left Alabama together after the national title and were each picked in the top 10 of the 2021 NFL draft, with Waddle going No. 6 to the Dolphins and Surtain being selected three picks later by the Broncos.

 
 'And then, it really happened' 
 Now in his sixth season, Surtain has ascended to the summit of NFL cornerbacks, voted as the league's best CB in an ESPN survey of NFL coaches, personnel executives and scouts during the offseason. At 26 years old, Surtain already has four Pro Bowl selections, two first-team All-Pro nominations and a 2024 Defensive Player of the Year award on his résumé. And Waddle, who turned 28 on Wednesday, was the Broncos' must-have addition this past offseason -- he had three 1,000-yard seasons in Miami and led the league in yards per catch in 2022.

 Before the March trade, the thought of being teammates again was a hopeful what-if -- an idea friends have as they contemplate the future in a profession where time isn't on anyone's side.

 "When we were at Bama, you might talk about what you hope happens, how it might happen and all that," Surtain said. "But you know the league, how it goes. I had seen with my dad, thinking you could end up in the same place wasn't really in that mix. You think about it, you want it, but the reality of it doesn't always match."

 They had shared an NFL field only once prior to this season, during the infamous 70-20 Dolphins win over Denver in Week 3 of the 2023 season. The two exchanged jerseys after that game, but thoughts that they would be together on the same NFL roster were confined to random musings.

 "You might think about it in a text or something," Surtain said.

 The Broncos had actually tinkered with the idea of a trade for Waddle during the 2025 season, but a deal never materialized. They reconsidered as the new league year began, seeking out more playmakers for quarterback Bo Nix .

 

 "We'd say, like, what if or how it would be a big thing," Waddle said. "But the NFL, to think it might happen, you want it to, but that's just out there.

 "And then, it really happened."

 The Broncos formally announced their acquisition of Waddle on March 18. And as the receiver started to work through all of the things he would need to do before joining a new team -- "you start thinking right away, about where you're going to live, packing all your stuff, all of it," he said -- he knew who he would call first.

 "That was a great call," Surtain said. "The best kind. ... I was just going through a day, getting work in and you get that call. Funny in this league, so much happens when you get a call, you get drafted, or sign [a contract], this was one of those calls for me. The best kind."

 
 'We do actually care about each other' 
 Waddle's arrival on a team that finished 14-3 last season and advanced to the AFC Championship Game had an all-in vibe to it. The Broncos knew what he could bring to their offense.

 But they got an added benefit they really didn't understand until on-field practices started in their offseason program -- the energy Waddle would bring in concert with Surtain with their individual personalities and shared dynamic. Their current teammates say Waddle is a high-volume talker, with wit and timing, whereas Surtain might be far more selective about when the words come out.

 But their personalities meld a bit when they face each other on the field. Surtain even admits that his teammates "maybe see me talk a little more" when he faces Waddle on the practice field than they had seen in his previous five NFL seasons.

 Despite the banter, the line…

title: Betting Broncos-Steelers: How will Pittsburgh respond to stunning events?
summary: Odds, analysis and recommended plays to help you bet the day after Thanksgiving game between the Broncos and Steelers.
full_text:
Let's put Aaron Rodgers on Black Friday, the NFL thought. Think again!

 Tuesday night's surprising news that the Pittsburgh Steelers were benching Aaron Rodgers in favor of Mason Rudolph -- and Rodgers' ensuing scorched-earth interview with Pat McAfee on Wednesday before then being cut by the team -- changed both the lineup and tenor of Friday's contest.

 But despite the vibes being in a very different place between the 8-2 Denver Broncos and the 6-4 Steelers, these teams are not as far apart as one might think. The Broncos rank 15th and 14th in offensive and defensive EPA per play, respectively (with that defensive number being particularly surprising!). The Steelers rank 21st and 10th in the same categories. Just something to keep in mind as we turn our attention to picks for Friday's game.

 

 

 

 Betting outlook 
 Here's an unconventional take from ESPN's Football Power Index : the Steelers' chance of winning Friday went up by benching Rodgers for Rudolph. Even outside of the Mike McCarthy/Rodgers drama, the reality of the situation is that Rodgers has played poorly in 2026 (as has been the case for years), with him ranking 26th out of 30 quarterbacks in QBR this year.

 

 I would not go as far as FPI -- which makes this game almost a pick 'em with Rudolph at the helm -- because perhaps there's some truth to Rodgers' criticisms of McCarthy and his playcalling and also because I think that's an awful lot of confidence in Rudolph. If I had to pick a side (and, full disclosure, I almost never do), I suppose I would go Steelers +4.5. But I won't.

 Instead, I'm going to think about tail outcomes here. What if things actually are as bad as Rodgers said? Or what if, even if exaggerated, the late quarterback switch and ensuing drama plays a big role in the team's preparation for Friday? Does that make a blowout loss more likely than a normal game? That seems possible to me. So let's play an alternate line and go Broncos -13.5 at +323 .

 

 Notable player props, bets 
 

 Note: Odds by DraftKings   and subject to change. 

 

 Jonah Coleman receptions OVER 3.5 (+106) 

 We're employing one of my favorite betting angles here: running back reception overs against a zone-heavy team. Running backs catch passes against zone coverage 15% of the time, compared to just 8% of the time against man. That's a huge difference! In back testing I've found that that isn't fully captured by the market, so in extreme cases I believe it's worth betting. And this is an extreme case, because the Steelers run zone 78% of the time -- the most of any team.

title: The Aaron Rodgers-Steelers marriage was always bound to end this way
summary: Rodgers was released by the Steelers after making accusations about Mike McCarthy. It's not his first breakup, and Pittsburgh should have seen it coming.
full_text:
At the peak of his powers, you could certainly argue that no one in the history of the NFL had ever slung a football -- we are talking pure passing ability -- better than Aaron Rodgers .

 His 122.5 passer rating in 2011 is the league's highest ever. In 2020, he completed 70.7% of his passes, accuracy that helped produce 48 touchdowns against just five interceptions. On any given night, there was breathtaking magic. Think of the 31-for-36, three-TD performance he put on  Atlanta  in the 2010 playoffs en route to a Super Bowl title, or the 2014 game against  Chicago  in which he threw for six touchdowns ... in the first half.

 When you're that good for that long -- Rodgers won four MVPs -- you, understandably, develop a superhuman belief in yourself.

 

 So much so that you believe you can not only lead the  Pittsburgh Steelers  to the Super Bowl in a season in which you turn 43 years old but that if you happen to lose consecutive games along the way, the problem is with the coach or the game plan or who knows what else. It's certainly not that you suddenly rank 26th in yards per attempt (6.2) but fourth in times sacked (31).

 Maybe this week, this implosion was inevitable. Rodgers demanded new game plans, more freedom to call plays and less influence from coach Mike McCarthy, with whom he once won big in Green Bay before sharing a messy breakup (but he recommended that Pittsburgh hire him anyway).

 "If you try to bench me, or don't change the playcalling, you should release me," Rodgers later said he told McCarthy while appearing on "The Pat McAfee Show."

 McCarthy chose the benching, replacing Rodgers, an eventual first-ballot Hall of Famer, with Mason Rudolph , a career second-stringer (just 19 starts across seven seasons).

 "There was an ultimatum made, clearly outside of his job description," McCarthy said Wednesday. "So it was my decision to bench him."

 So, yes, maybe this is how it was destined to end: Rodgers going on with McAfee, throwing different kinds of bombs, taking one last daring shot to the corner of the end zone to pull out victory or go down in flames. He detailed how McCarthy gave Pittsburgh a halftime pep talk by shouting "1-2-3 Packers." He said McCarthy was always behind on watching game film. He implied his coach was too tired to still do this job.

 "Mike came in [to a meeting] late, sat down, and within 10 minutes began snoring," Rodgers said. "He woke himself up. ... Five minutes later, you hear the snoring again."

 Some of it -- the poor film study, for instance -- was concerning. Some of it was, eh, whatever -- a gaffe in a halftime speech would be funny, if the Steelers hadn't lost to lowly  Philadelphia  that day.

 

 McCarthy acknowledged some of it and didn't bother to address the rest. He said he was the right man to coach the Steelers because, "I know how to win, and that's the facts," although the facts note that he has only ever really won in the postseason with Rodgers as his QB. Five seasons in Dallas (2020 to 2024) yielded just one playoff victory.

 Most notable was the scorched-earth aspect of it all; Rodgers burned every bridge in a city known for bridges and brought pandemonium to a franchise that prides itself on professionalism.

 "I don't care. What are you going to do to me?" Rodgers said. "... You're going to release me? Cool."

 Pittsburgh chose to release him, even at 6-4 and with plenty to play for. It was a particularly spectacular ending to a partnership that never made much sense to begin with.

 The Steelers hoped they could get vintage Rodgers on the field and a maturing presence who would conform to their preferred culture off it. Instead, they got the entire Rodgers experience: the news conferences, the grievances, the carefully constructed explanations, the podcast appearances, the sense that every disagreement is part of a much larger philosophical battle.

 Rodgers, meanwhile, was desperate for a team and rarely seems to believe the volatile fights he finds himself in are of his making. Although, in fairness, he did take some blame for recommending McCarthy.

 "I'm not a victim here," Rodgers said. "I am accountable."

 

 Who is more at fault hardly matters -- this is Rodgers' third ugly professional breakup, with hard feelings and tough words on his way out of Green Bay and New York . What was supposed to be a storybook finish instead broke the way it tends to break with Rodgers.

 For a long, glorious stretch, there might never have been a more talented quarterback than Aaron Rodgers.

 If you hang on long enough, though, and never accept the reality of diminishing performance, eventually the talent stops being worth the trouble. That probably came a while ago for Rodgers. Pittsburgh needed a little longer to figure it out.

 The Steelers thought they could steal one last championship run. Instead, they got one last season of drama from the Aaron Rodgers reality show.

title: Why the Seahawks are turning back to quarterback Sam Darnold vs. the 49ers
summary: Drew Lock has been 'fantastic' filling in for Darnold, who has struggled with injuries but is on track to face 9-1 San Francisco on Sunday.
full_text:
RENTON, Wash. -- Having coached Ben Roethlisberger and the Pittsburgh Steelers to a Super Bowl title 18 years ago, Mike Tomlin was speaking from experience when he weighed in on the Seattle Seahawks ' quarterback situation.

 Hours after backup  Drew Lock  led Seattle to a 21-13 win over the Las Vegas Raiders on Nov. 15 -- his fourth victory in as many fill-in appearances this season -- Tomlin correctly predicted during the "Sunday Night Football" broadcast that coach Mike Macdonald would turn back to beleaguered starter Sam Darnold after the Seahawks' bye.

 Tomlin said the Seahawks coach and quarterback were "tied together for life," and that if he were in Macdonald's shoes, he'd stick with Darnold "because of the emotional bank account" he built last season while helping Seattle win Super Bowl LX .

 "I think he's spot on," Macdonald said the next day after hearing the Tomlin clip on his Seattle Sports 710-AM radio show.

 That helps explain why Darnold -- who was a full participant in practice Wednesday and Thursday --  will be back in the starting lineup Sunday when Seattle (6-4) faces the NFC West-leading San Francisco 49ers (9-1) at Levi's Stadium in a game the Seahawks must win to keep any hope of staying in the division race  alive.

 As predictable as Macdonald's decision might have been, it hardly seemed straightforward.

 

 Whereas Lock has played some of the best football of his career in relief this season, Darnold has been shaky in between two stints on the sideline due to injuries. The "bank account" that Tomlin mentioned isn't drained, but it saw more withdrawals than deposits as Darnold quarterbacked Seattle to a 2-4 record after returning from the glute injury that knocked him out of the season opener on the fifth play and kept him out the next game.

 From Week 3 to Week 8, Darnold threw nine interceptions and 10 touchdown passes while posting a Total QBR of 50.1 that ranked 23rd in that span. To be fair, a couple of his interceptions entailed some tough luck, with deflected passes getting picked in losses to the Washington Commanders and Chicago Bears . But others were backbreakers.

 In Week 3, Darnold threw a pick-six when he underestimated a breaking Commanders defender. On both of his late interceptions in an overtime loss to the Denver Broncos three weeks later, he bypassed an open receiver in the flat before forcing throws downfield.

 Even the best performance of the season for Darnold and the Seahawks' offense -- a 20-3 victory over the previously unbeaten Kansas City Chiefs in Week 7 -- included a regrettable mistake by the quarterback, who was intercepted on a needlessly risky throw into the end zone. A week after that signature win over Kansas City, the Bears beat the Seahawks 34-17 for their most lopsided defeat in almost two years. Darnold played through a cracked rib he suffered on his first dropback of the game, then injured his quad late in the fourth quarter.

 Lock, meanwhile, has quarterbacked the Seahawks to twice as many wins this season in two fewer games than Darnold. He has thrown seven touchdown passes and zero interceptions, with his only two turnovers coming on lost fumbles against the Raiders. And one was on a fluky play in which running back Zach Charbonnet bumped into the quarterback while he was starting his delivery.

 Lock's Total QBR of 92.4 in that game was his third best in eight NFL seasons. By that metric, his other three performances were also among the best of his career -- 76.9 against the New England Patriots in Week 1 (eighth), 82.7 against the Arizona Cardinals in Week 2 (seventh) and 89.3 against Arizona in Week 9 (fourth).

 

 Lock's Total QBR this season is 86.1. That includes the league's sixth-best mark over the first two weeks (79.9) and second best over Weeks 9-10 (90.7), when he played through injuries to his oblique and right elbow.

 "Drew's been fantastic, he's been phenomenal," Macdonald said. "But Sam's our quarterback."

 Darnold might not have an endless leash, but beyond the equity he built last season, the context of 2026 helps explain why he's back in the starting lineup.

 Lock's performances came against defenses that entered Week 12 ranked 31st (Arizona), 29th (Las Vegas) and 26th (New England) in EPA. The defenses Darnold faced ranked third (Kansas City), seventh (Chicago), ninth (San Francisco), 12th (Denver), 18th (L.A. Chargers) and 22nd (Washington) in EPA over the first 11 weeks. With Charbonnet and Jadarian Price together in the backfield, Lock benefitted in his past two starts from an emerging run game, something Darnold has yet to enjoy.

 Even with the bad interception, Darnold's Total QBR of 93.4 against Kansas City was the fourth best of his nine-year career. His QBR of 50.1 in six full games this season is still considerably better than his 35.7 mark over the final eight weeks of the 2025 regular season, which ranked 27th. Darnold had led the league with a 78.2 QBR over the first 10 weeks of last season.

 So instead of benching Darnold, Macdonald and the Seahawks' offensive coaches are taking it upon themselves to get him back to a level of play they've seen him reach.

 "I think making sure that we have a really clear idea of how we want to operate coming out of this bye week on who we want to be and how we want to get there," Macdonald said when asked how Seattle's coaches can help Darnold. "I think we have a good, clear vision right now, but making sure we can maximize the alignment coming down the home stretch here where we can hunt out any inconsistencies on things that we're asking our offense to do, especially our quarterback, and be really clear on the identity that we want to come to life.

 

 "I think that'll help everybody, especially Sam."

 Another likely reason why Macdonald is sticking with Darnold is that he has seen the quarterback deliver in big games, including two late last season against the 49ers. Seattle beat them in Week 18, with the NFC West title and conference's No. 1 seed on the line, and then in the divisional round of the playoff as he played through an oblique injury.

 The stakes aren't as high Sunday, but it's still a pivotal game. A season sweep by San Francisco would bury the Seahawks in the NFC West race, putting them four games back with six to go. They also need a win to avoid losing any ground in the wild-card standings, with Seattle and four other teams vying for three spots.

 As for Darnold, he needs to make a deposit in the metaphorical bank account that Tomlin mentioned, lest it gets any lower.

title: Can the 49ers lock up the NFC West after exceeding preseason expectations?
summary: The 49ers are 9-1, and two of their next three games are against the Seahawks (6-4) and Rams (7-4) at home.
full_text:
SANTA CLARA, Calif. -- For a team with four NFC Championship Games and two Super Bowl appearances since 2019 -- and the majority of the core that took it to those heights still in place -- the San Francisco 49ers entered this season widely considered the third-best team ... in their own division.

 After a series of bold roster moves, including trades for edge rusher Myles Garrett and cornerback Trent McDuffie , the Los Angeles Rams were the chic pick to win the NFC West and Super Bowl. The defending champion Seattle Seahawks  were right on their heels. The Niners, despite finishing 12-5 and winning a road playoff game in January, were an afterthought.

 While that might have angered some of their most devout believers, it suited their locker room just fine.

 "I think it's helped a lot," left tackle Trent Williams said. "That's kind of how you want things to be. Nobody likes all the attention and all the expectations and whatnot. They'd be lying if they said they did. I think not having all that swirling around us just allowed us to focus on football."

 That low-profile luxury has officially expired. At 9-1, San Francisco has surged from a 21.5% preseason chance to win the division and a 4.7% shot at the Super Bowl, per ESPN Analytics, to the overwhelming favorite in both. The 49ers have a 98.2% chance to capture the NFC West and a 29.4% chance to hoist the Lombardi Trophy -- nearly double the next closest team, the Buffalo Bills .

 

 Now the 49ers enter a pivotal stretch, featuring home games against the Seahawks and Rams , as well as a road trip to face the Giants . The biggest test for the rest of the regular season? Readjusting to life as the hunted rather than the hunter.

 "We know how we've been so far, but we're halfway there and we've got a long way to go," coach Kyle Shanahan said.

 Maintaining that spot atop the NFL's hierarchy starts with quarterback Brock Purdy , who is playing some of the best football of his career. Although injuries have ravaged the receiver corps, forcing Purdy and Shanahan to devise creative ways to move the ball and score points, it hasn't slowed them down.

 The 49ers rank first in the NFL in points per game (31.6) and offensive efficiency (79.91). They're also second in offensive expected points added (109.22), per NFL Next Gen Stats.

 Purdy is quick to say those numbers reflect a cumulative effort by Shanahan, his staff and everyone on offense. But Purdy's steady hand has been the driving force behind everything the team has accomplished. He leads the NFL in QBR (84.2), yards per attempt (9.0) and yards per drop back (8.52); he ranks top three in completion percentage (71%) and passing touchdowns (23).

 After Sunday night's 35-10 demolition of the Vikings and their vaunted defense -- bolstering Purdy's Most Valuable Player case -- running back Christian McCaffrey called him "one of the best players I've ever played with." Wide receiver Mike Evans took it a step further, calling Purdy the "best player in the game."

 "Brock plays the right way," Shanahan said. "He just truly plays the position. ... Brock keeps a clear mind and just plays each play one at a time and does what he's supposed to do. If nothing's there or he can't see something or something doesn't work, then he tries to compete and make a play on his own."

 

 Purdy's approach has set the tone for the rest of the roster, which has once again leaned on its depth to keep the train on the tracks. Evans' return from Achilles tendinitis provided a major spark against the Vikings -- he posted six catches for 109 yards and a touchdown -- though the 49ers will have to manage his workload carefully to keep him healthy down the stretch.

 Promising rookie wideout  De'Zhaun Stribling  could also return in December from ankle surgery after recently doing resistance-band work on a side field during practice. On defense, the team activated cornerback Nate Hobbs  from injured reserve this week.

 The 49ers were also aggressive at the trade deadline by adding defensive tackle DeForest Buckner and wide receiver Keenan Allen  -- proven veterans capable of immediately fortifying injury-riddled positions. And another calculated move: keeping backup quarterback Mac Jones for injury insurance on Purdy rather than trading him for a pick that wouldn't help this season's team.

 Just as San Francisco's luck started trending up, it suffered a major blow at right tackle: Colton McKivitz fractured and dislocated his left ankle against the Vikings and will almost certainly miss the rest of the season. He ranked first among 65 qualifying tackles in pass block win rate, and opposing defenses will undoubtedly test his replacement ( Vederian Lowe ) in the coming weeks. Purdy is also dealing with an ankle injury that popped up in the second quarter of the win against Minnesota. 

 Still, San Francisco's history of battling attrition has hardened the locker room to the reality of NFL injuries and what it takes to overcome them.

 "I think it's a very mature team," McCaffrey said. "Adversity is really a word, but it's kind of just normal. You don't get too high; you don't get too low. When something bad happens, you don't look at it as something bad happening. You just deal with it and move on, and you don't talk about it a lot.

 "I think that's one thing that's cool about our culture in general is mistakes are going to be made, things are going to happen, but football, that's what makes it fun. I think we got guys with the right mentality and enough maturity to correct mistakes, capitalize on strengths and just keep moving forward."

 

 This week, the Niners turn their attention back to the Seahawks, who come off a bye eager to avenge their Week 5 loss in Seattle . San Francisco, meanwhile, returns from a grueling road trip that included stops in Dallas  and Colorado Springs and a primetime game in Mexico City.

 The stakes for both sides are significant. A 49ers win pushes their chances of winning the NFC West to 99.7% while dropping Seattle's postseason chances from to 36.3%, per ESPN Analytics. A Seahawks victory would vault their playoff hopes to 62.3%.

 With the NFC East-leading Giants and a rematch against the Rams looming right after, the Niners will learn plenty about their playoff positioning by mid-December. But if they continue this hot streak -- one that has included their most wins by 20-plus points since 2012 -- the NFC's No. 1 seed is well within their reach. ESPN Analytics currently gives them 82.4% odds.

 Still, Shanahan is quick to acknowledge there's plenty of football left to play. Following the win in Mexico City, he was asked whether this is the best team he has coached since taking over the 49ers in 2017. He said no, though he didn't rule out the possibility that it could eventually get there.

 "We've got to earn that," Shanahan said. "We've done some good things. But it's still to be determined."

 After all, nobody knows better than these Niners how fast a team can go from afterthought to favorite.
